screens.title: Optimizing Queries with EXPLAIN
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will make EXPLAIN your primary diagnostic tool for query performance. EXPLAIN shows the execution plan MySQL intends to use for a SELECT statement. That plan reveals access methods, which indexes the optimizer considered and chose, estimated row counts, and important flags in the Extra column that often point directly to slow operations such as filesort or temporary tables. Knowing how to read EXPLAIN means you stop guessing and start fixing. For example, if EXPLAIN shows a type of ALL and Extra of Using filesort, you know you likely need a composite index covering the WHERE and ORDER BY. If the plan shows Using index, that tells you MySQL can satisfy the query from the index alone, which is ideal for read-heavy operations. Over the next screens we will define each critical column, practice reading real EXPLAIN output, run a small optimization cycle on a sample query, and highlight common mistakes. By the end you’ll be confident identifying whether a query does a full table scan, which index to add, and how to validate changes by re-running EXPLAIN. Think of EXPLAIN as a roadmap: it doesn’t change data, but it shows where to invest your tuning effort.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › Optimizing Queries with EXPLAIN
Optimizing Queries with EXPLAIN
Turn execution plans into concrete optimizations: identify scans, index opportunities, and bottlenecks.
In this lesson

You will learn how to read EXPLAIN output, interpret key columns like type and Extra, and form index-based fixes that improve query latency.

Why it matters

Wrong plan choices cause heavy I/O, disk sorts, and temporary tables. EXPLAIN points to the exact component that is wasting resources.

Explore Key Topics
Reading EXPLAIN
Understand id, type, key, rows and Extra to locate bottlenecks.
Access Types
Learn the ranking from ALL to const and why you prefer ref/eq_ref/range.
Index Fixes
Design composite indexes to cover WHERE and ORDER BY and re-check EXPLAIN.
EXPLAIN output snapshot
Each row represents an operation; columns reveal access and costs.
id | select_type | table | type | key | rows | Extra
1 | SIMPLE | products | ALL | NULL | 100000 | Using filesort
Quick fix
Create composite index that matches WHERE and ORDER BY to avoid filesort and full scan.
Common pitfall
Don’t assume a good-looking plan equals fast execution; always measure after changes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you will use immediately as a DBA. First, you will master the EXPLAIN statement so you can generate a readable execution plan for any SELECT. That skill matters because EXPLAIN is a non-destructive way to inspect how MySQL intends to access data, and it gives you the evidence to choose an optimization. Second, you will interpret core EXPLAIN columns — id, select_type, table, type, key, rows, and Extra — and explain what each value implies about access patterns. Being fluent with these columns lets you detect full scans, index usage, and whether a query will sort or build a temporary table. Third, you will recognize inefficient access methods such as ALL or index and understand their performance implications so you can prioritize fixes. Finally, you will identify Extra column warnings like Using filesort or Using temporary and translate them into corrective actions, most often by designing appropriate indexes. Each objective ties to a verification milestone so you can confirm competency by re-running EXPLAIN after making an indexed change and observing improved access types or removal of costly Extra flags.

Learning Objectives
A four-step competency map from reading plans to applying index fixes.
01
Master EXPLAIN

Run EXPLAIN on SELECT queries and read the plan to identify access patterns. This skill is safe to run on production and gives you visibility before changing schema or indexes.

Mnemonic: magnifying glass over the plan
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

Interpret EXPLAIN columns

Spot inefficient access

Detect access types like ALL or index that force scans, and prioritize queries that read many rows. Understanding access types helps you pick targeted indexing strategies.

Resolve Extra flags

Interpret Extra values like Using filesort or Using temporary and translate them into index or query rewrites to remove heavy sorts or temp tables.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice Focus
screens.narratorSegment: This companion objectives slide emphasizes validation and the practical checklist you will use after making changes. You will learn to compare EXPLAIN results before and after an index or query change, focusing on changes in type, key, rows, and Extra. This comparison proves whether the optimization reduced row estimates, removed filesorts, or enabled a covering index. You will also practice translating EXPLAIN signals into concrete actions: e. g., when type is ALL and Extra shows Using filesort, design a composite index that covers the WHERE and ORDER BY columns. Next, you will learn to avoid common misreads such as trusting type alone without looking at rows or Extra. Finally, you will confirm that a better plan in EXPLAIN corresponds to better runtime by running the actual query and checking response time and resource usage. These verification steps complete the optimization loop and ensure you make safe, measurable improvements in a staging environment before altering production systems.

Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › Learning Objectives — Practice
Compare plans before and after

Capture EXPLAIN output for the original query, apply a proposed index, then run EXPLAIN again to confirm that type, key, rows, or Extra have improved.

Before: type=ALL, Extra=Using filesort
After: type=ref, key=idx_city_lastname, Extra=Using index
Measure runtime

Plan changes are necessary but not sufficient. Run the actual SELECT to ensure latency and resource use improve after schema changes.

Mnemonic: before/after stopwatch
Common verification checklist
  • Confirm key changed from NULL to a named index.
  • Confirm type moved from ALL/index to ref/eq_ref/range.
  • Confirm Extra removed filesort or temporary when possible.
  • Run the SELECT to confirm lower execution time and I/O.

screens.title: What EXPLAIN shows and why it’s safe
screens.narratorSegment: EXPLAIN is a read-only statement that outputs the execution plan for a SELECT. It does not run the query to return all rows; instead it returns a structured description of steps MySQL plans to take, one row per table operation. That structure includes identifiers and descriptors such as id and select_type which show query block order, and it includes access details about how each table will be scanned or indexed. The ability to see the plan safely is valuable: you can iteratively change schema or index design in staging, re-run EXPLAIN, and measure impact without touching production data. A useful mental model is to think of EXPLAIN as a rehearsal — it tells you the cast and choreography before the performance. One misconception to avoid is thinking EXPLAIN reports actual execution time; it reports the optimizer’s planned strategy and row estimates, not wall-clock duration. Therefore, always validate a plan change by executing the query to confirm throughput and latency improvements. To practice, prepend EXPLAIN to a SELECT and inspect each row in the returned table. That disciplined process moves optimization from guesswork to evidence-based changes.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › What EXPLAIN shows
Definition and safety

EXPLAIN returns the optimizer’s plan for a SELECT statement without executing the full query. It lists operations per table and supplies estimates and flags you can act on.

How to run
EXPLAIN SELECT ...
Misconception
EXPLAIN shows planned work and estimates, not actual execution time. Always validate after optimization by running the query.
EXPLAIN output example
id | select_type | table | type | possible_keys | key | rows | Extra
1 | SIMPLE | customers | ALL | NULL | NULL | 1000000 | Using filesort
Practice tip
Run EXPLAIN first, then change indexes, then re-run to see the plan change before you update production schema.

screens.title: How to run EXPLAIN and read the id and select_type columns
screens.narratorSegment: Start with a simple SELECT and prepend EXPLAIN. The output’s id column labels query blocks: a single SELECT typically has id 1, while subqueries and derived tables produce multiple ids that indicate execution order. The select_type column complements id by describing the role of each SELECT row — values like SIMPLE, PRIMARY, SUBQUERY, DERIVED, or UNION tell you whether the row is the outer query, a subquery, or a derived table. Understanding id and select_type helps you reason about join order and whether a costly subquery will be run multiple times. For example, if you see a SUBQUERY with a high rows estimate, that may indicate repeated execution and an opportunity to rewrite the query as a join or materialized derived table. A common mistake is to ignore select_type when multiple ids appear; doing so hides the fact that a nested subquery could dominate cost even if the outer table looks efficient. Practice by running EXPLAIN on queries that include subselects and compare the id ordering to the expected logical flow. The goal is to spot unexpected nested work so you can refactor the query into a more efficient shape.

keyIdea.title: Query block roles
keyIdea.text: id and select_type reveal the execution order and whether a row represents the outer query, a subquery, or a derived table — crucial for spotting repeated expensive work.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › id and select_type
Run example
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT id FROM vip_customers);
Expected output shows multiple ids: one for the outer SELECT and one for the SUBQUERY. Compare select_type values to confirm which block is which.
Practice
Run EXPLAIN on queries with nested selects and note which id corresponds to the repeating or expensive block.
Key points
  • id orders execution; higher-level rows may refer to nested operations.
  • select_type describes the role: SIMPLE, PRIMARY, SUBQUERY, DERIVED, UNION.
  • A SUBQUERY with high rows estimate can be a performance hotspot.
Misread to avoid
Don’t assume id alone tells cost; always read select_type alongside rows and type to understand impact.

screens.title: Access types explained: ALL → index → range → ref → eq_ref → const
screens.narratorSegment: The type column is one of the most critical indicators of how MySQL will access a table, and it has an order from worst to best. At the low end, ALL means a full table scan — MySQL will read every row, which is almost always costly on large tables. index is a full index scan: it reads the entire index but avoids reading full rows, so it’s a bit better than ALL. range uses an index to find rows within a value range and is generally good for predicates with inequality or IN lists. ref means matching rows are found via a non-unique index or an index prefix; it is efficient when multiple rows per key are acceptable. eq_ref is used for joins when a unique or primary key is compared; MySQL retrieves at most one matching row per lookup and this is very efficient. At the top are const and system where MySQL can treat the table as a constant or single-row, which is fastest. When you inspect EXPLAIN, aim for ref, eq_ref, range, const where possible for the hot paths. A common mistake is to assume range is bad; in many cases range is perfectly acceptable compared to index or ALL. Use these access types to prioritize where to add or adjust indexes.

keyIdea.title: Access type ranking
keyIdea.text: Aim for ref, eq_ref, range, const; avoid ALL and full index scans when working with large datasets.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › Access types
Access types and impact
ALL
Full table scan. Avoid on large tables; indicates no useful index was used.
index
Full index scan; better than ALL but still expensive if large.
range
Index range scan for inequalities or IN lists. Generally good.
ref
Non-unique index lookup; efficient for many-to-one relationships.
eq_ref
Unique index or primary key join; retrieves at most one row per lookup and is very efficient.
const/system
Single-row reads treated as constants; fastest possible access.
When range is fine
Range is suitable for queries with BETWEEN or IN; prefer it over index or ALL when indexes can narrow results effectively.
Common pitfall
Do not look at type in isolation; a range with large rows estimate may still be costly compared to targeted eq_ref joins.
Takeaway
Use access type as a priority signal: convert ALL/index scans into range/ref/eq_ref by adding suitable indexes or rewriting joins.

screens.title: Indexes in EXPLAIN: possible_keys, key, key_len, and ref
screens.narratorSegment: EXPLAIN provides a window into index selection through possible_keys, key, key_len, and ref. possible_keys lists indexes the optimizer could consider for the table; it’s your hint about opportunities where an index might help. key shows the index actually chosen by the optimizer. If key is NULL, no index was used, which often explains a type of ALL. key_len indicates how many bytes of the index MySQL used; for composite indexes this tells you how many leading columns are part of the match. ref displays which column or constant is compared to that index, revealing why the index matched. A useful diagnostic step is to check possible_keys when key is NULL: if possible_keys is empty, you may need to create an index. If possible_keys lists an index but key is different or NULL, examine why the optimizer avoided it — sometimes column order in a composite index or data distribution matters. Avoid the mistake of assuming any index will be used; index design must match the WHERE and ORDER BY patterns. When you alter indexes, re-run EXPLAIN and confirm key changes from NULL to a named index and key_len shows expected usage of composite parts.

keyIdea.text: possible_keys suggests candidate indexes; key shows the chosen index; key_len and ref explain how much and which part of a composite index was used.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › Indexes in EXPLAIN
Which indexes were considered and used
possible_keys: idx_city, idx_name key: idx_city key_len: 12 ref: const
If key is NULL, MySQL did not use an index for that table. If possible_keys is empty, create an index aligned to the query pattern.
Composite index hint
key_len helps you see whether a composite index’s leading columns were used. If key_len is shorter than expected, reorder or split the index to match WHERE and ORDER BY.
Misconception
possible_keys alone does not mean the optimizer will use those indexes; key shows the final choice and reveals missed opportunities.
Action
When key is NULL and possible_keys is empty, create an index that matches filtering and ordering columns, then re-run EXPLAIN to validate key changes.

screens.title: rows and filtered: estimated work and selectivity
screens.narratorSegment: The rows column in EXPLAIN is an estimate of how many rows MySQL expects to examine to produce results for that table operation. Lower estimates generally indicate less work and lower cost. filtered expresses an estimated percentage of rows that pass the table-level condition; a higher filtered percentage is better because it means the condition is selective. These estimates come from table statistics and data distribution; they can be inaccurate if statistics are stale or data distribution is skewed. Use rows and filtered to prioritize fixes: an access type of range paired with millions in rows might still be a performance problem. A common mistake is to focus only on type and ignore rows; the combination of both gives a more accurate picture of cost. If rows is high, consider adding or refining indexes, rewriting the query, or adding more selective predicates. After making changes, refresh statistics and re-run EXPLAIN to confirm that rows and filtered improve, which usually translates into lower execution work when you subsequently run the query. rows and filtered: estimated work and selectivity means rows and filtered are optimizer estimates that guide where to apply indexing or query rewrites; always validate with real query runs after changes.. In practical terms, how estimated row counts and percentage filtering guide optimization priority. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › rows and filtered
Estimated rows and selectivity

rows is MySQL’s estimate of rows to read; filtered is the percentage expected to match the condition. Both derive from statistics and affect the optimizer’s cost model.

Example: rows = 1000000, filtered = 1.00 means many rows scanned but only 1% kept, implying heavy work to filter.
If rows stays high after indexing, consider rewriting the query or improving statistics.
Practical step
After adding an index, run ANALYZE TABLE or let auto-update statistics run, then re-run EXPLAIN to see corrected rows and filtered values.
Misconception
Don’t assume a low rows estimate always means fast execution; confirm by running the query and checking I/O and latency.
Takeaway
Use rows and filtered to prioritize queries with high expected work; then apply index or rewrite strategies and measure actual performance.

screens.title: Extra column flags: Using filesort, Using temporary, and Using index
screens.narratorSegment: The Extra column often holds the clearest clues to hidden bottlenecks. "Using filesort" means MySQL must perform an extra pass to sort results because an index could not satisfy the ORDER BY. This can be expensive for large result sets. "Using temporary" indicates MySQL created a temporary table, frequently for GROUP BY or DISTINCT, and this can cause disk input and output if the temporary spills to disk. "Using index" is a positive flag meaning a covering index was used so the storage engine did not need to read full data rows. "Using where" simply means a WHERE clause was applied; when combined with ALL it tells you the engine applied the filter after scanning, which is inefficient. "Using index condition" shows that MySQL pushed down conditions into the storage engine to filter using the index, which can improve efficiency. A common trap is assuming Using index always means the plan is perfect; it indicates no row lookup was necessary but other tables or clauses may still be costly. Use the Extra column together with type and rows to diagnose and prioritize fixes like adding a composite index to eliminate filesort or avoid temporary table creation.

keyIdea.title: Extra reveals traps
keyIdea.text: Extra flags such as Using filesort or Using temporary point to operations that often cause disk I/O; Using index indicates a covering index and is usually desirable.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › Extra column flags
Common Extra values
  • Using filesort: indicates an extra sort pass; often fixed by an index that matches ORDER BY.
  • Using temporary: temporary table was required; review GROUP BY, DISTINCT, or derived-table usage.
  • Using index: covering index used; efficient when SELECT list is satisfied by the index.
  • Using where: WHERE applied; combined with ALL suggests filtering after scanning.
  • Using index condition: predicate pushed to storage engine; good for selective index filtering.
Example diagnosis
If you see type=ALL and Extra=Using filesort, create or reorder an index to cover WHERE and ORDER BY to avoid the filesort and reduce scanned rows.
Misconception
Using index means no row lookups for those columns, but the overall query may still scan other tables or invoke temporary tables elsewhere in the plan.
Practical tip
When Extra shows filesort or temporary, design a composite index that covers filtering and sorting columns, then re-run EXPLAIN and validate that the Extra flags change or disappear.

screens.title: Practical example: products ORDER BY price and adding a composite index
screens.narratorSegment: Let’s work through a concrete example from the chapter. Suppose products has product_id, category_id, price and you run a query filtered by category_id and ordered by price. Running EXPLAIN may show type = ALL and Extra = Using filesort. That indicates a full table scan and an expensive sort pass. A direct corrective action is to create a composite index on category_id and price. A suitable index often looks like an index with category first and price second because WHERE filters by category_id while ORDER BY sorts by price. After creating the index, re-run EXPLAIN. You should see type move to ref or range, key become the new composite index, and Extra change to Using index or no filesort. This shows the index can both filter and satisfy the ordering. Be mindful that if SELECT * is still used, MySQL may need to read rows to retrieve other columns, so Using index only appears when the index covers all required columns. Validate the runtime after the index change to confirm lower latency. This step-by-step exercise demonstrates how EXPLAIN points you to the exact index you need and how re-running the plan confirms the effectiveness of the change.

narration.text: Let’s work through a concrete example from the chapter. Suppose products has product_id, category_id, price and you run a query filtered by category_id and ordered by price. screens.narratorSegment: Turn diagnosis into a repeatable workflow. Step one: diagnose with EXPLAIN. Capture the plan and note type, key, rows, and Extra values for the slow query. screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: There are recurring mistakes that slow down optimization projects. First, focusing on the type column alone without checking rows and Extra can mislead you. For instance, a range access with a very large rows estimate can still be costly; likewise, seeing ref doesn’t automatically mean the overall plan is efficient. Second, treating EXPLAIN as a guarantee of runtime is incorrect; EXPLAIN reports planned operations and estimates. Always run the actual query after changes. Third, applying indexes blindly without staging or measurement can cause regressions because indexes add write cost and may change plans for other queries. Fourth, overlooking key_len and ref for composite indexes leads to partial index usage: the index must be ordered so its leading columns match filtering; otherwise MySQL will not use the full index. To avoid these mistakes, adopt a checklist: inspect type, rows, key, and Extra together; design indexes to match WHERE and ORDER BY; stage schema changes; and measure runtime before and after. This disciplined approach reduces wasted effort and produces reliable performance gains. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will make EXPLAIN your primary diagnostic tool for query performance. EXPLAIN shows the execution plan MySQL intends to use for a SELECT statement. That plan reveals access methods, which indexes the optimizer considered and chose, estimated row counts, and important flags in the Extra column that often point directly to slow operations such as filesort or temporary tables. Knowing how to read EXPLAIN means you stop guessing and start fixing. For example, if EXPLAIN shows a type of ALL and Extra of Using filesort, you know you likely need a composite index covering the WHERE and ORDER BY. If the plan shows Using index, that tells you MySQL can satisfy the query from the index alone, which is ideal for read-heavy operations. Over the next screens we will define each critical column, practice reading real EXPLAIN output, run a small optimization cycle on a sample query, and highlight common mistakes. By the end you’ll be confident identifying whether a query does a full table scan, which index to add, and how to validate changes by re-running EXPLAIN. Think of EXPLAIN as a roadmap: it doesn’t change data, but it shows where to invest your tuning effort.

These objectives map to practical skills you will use immediately as a DBA. First, you will master the EXPLAIN statement so you can generate a readable execution plan for any SELECT. That skill matters because EXPLAIN is a non-destructive way to inspect how MySQL intends to access data, and it gives you the evidence to choose an optimization. Second, you will interpret core EXPLAIN columns — id, select_type, table, type, key, rows, and Extra — and explain what each value implies about access patterns. Being fluent with these columns lets you detect full scans, index usage, and whether a query will sort or build a temporary table. Third, you will recognize inefficient access methods such as ALL or index and understand their performance implications so you can prioritize fixes. Finally, you will identify Extra column warnings like Using filesort or Using temporary and translate them into corrective actions, most often by designing appropriate indexes. Each objective ties to a verification milestone so you can confirm competency by re-running EXPLAIN after making an indexed change and observing improved access types or removal of costly Extra flags.

This companion objectives slide emphasizes validation and the practical checklist you will use after making changes. You will learn to compare EXPLAIN results before and after an index or query change, focusing on changes in type, key, rows, and Extra. This comparison proves whether the optimization reduced row estimates, removed filesorts, or enabled a covering index. You will also practice translating EXPLAIN signals into concrete actions: e. g., when type is ALL and Extra shows Using filesort, design a composite index that covers the WHERE and ORDER BY columns. Next, you will learn to avoid common misreads such as trusting type alone without looking at rows or Extra. Finally, you will confirm that a better plan in EXPLAIN corresponds to better runtime by running the actual query and checking response time and resource usage. These verification steps complete the optimization loop and ensure you make safe, measurable improvements in a staging environment before altering production systems.

EXPLAIN is a read-only statement that outputs the execution plan for a SELECT. It does not run the query to return all rows; instead it returns a structured description of steps MySQL plans to take, one row per table operation. That structure includes identifiers and descriptors such as id and select_type which show query block order, and it includes access details about how each table will be scanned or indexed. The ability to see the plan safely is valuable: you can iteratively change schema or index design in staging, re-run EXPLAIN, and measure impact without touching production data. A useful mental model is to think of EXPLAIN as a rehearsal — it tells you the cast and choreography before the performance. One misconception to avoid is thinking EXPLAIN reports actual execution time; it reports the optimizer’s planned strategy and row estimates, not wall-clock duration. Therefore, always validate a plan change by executing the query to confirm throughput and latency improvements. To practice, prepend EXPLAIN to a SELECT and inspect each row in the returned table. That disciplined process moves optimization from guesswork to evidence-based changes.

Start with a simple SELECT and prepend EXPLAIN. The output’s id column labels query blocks: a single SELECT typically has id 1, while subqueries and derived tables produce multiple ids that indicate execution order. The select_type column complements id by describing the role of each SELECT row — values like SIMPLE, PRIMARY, SUBQUERY, DERIVED, or UNION tell you whether the row is the outer query, a subquery, or a derived table. Understanding id and select_type helps you reason about join order and whether a costly subquery will be run multiple times. For example, if you see a SUBQUERY with a high rows estimate, that may indicate repeated execution and an opportunity to rewrite the query as a join or materialized derived table. A common mistake is to ignore select_type when multiple ids appear; doing so hides the fact that a nested subquery could dominate cost even if the outer table looks efficient. Practice by running EXPLAIN on queries that include subselects and compare the id ordering to the expected logical flow. The goal is to spot unexpected nested work so you can refactor the query into a more efficient shape.

The type column is one of the most critical indicators of how MySQL will access a table, and it has an order from worst to best. At the low end, ALL means a full table scan — MySQL will read every row, which is almost always costly on large tables. index is a full index scan: it reads the entire index but avoids reading full rows, so it’s a bit better than ALL. range uses an index to find rows within a value range and is generally good for predicates with inequality or IN lists. ref means matching rows are found via a non-unique index or an index prefix; it is efficient when multiple rows per key are acceptable. eq_ref is used for joins when a unique or primary key is compared; MySQL retrieves at most one matching row per lookup and this is very efficient. At the top are const and system where MySQL can treat the table as a constant or single-row, which is fastest. When you inspect EXPLAIN, aim for ref, eq_ref, range, const where possible for the hot paths. A common mistake is to assume range is bad; in many cases range is perfectly acceptable compared to index or ALL. Use these access types to prioritize where to add or adjust indexes.

EXPLAIN provides a window into index selection through possible_keys, key, key_len, and ref. possible_keys lists indexes the optimizer could consider for the table; it’s your hint about opportunities where an index might help. key shows the index actually chosen by the optimizer. If key is NULL, no index was used, which often explains a type of ALL. key_len indicates how many bytes of the index MySQL used; for composite indexes this tells you how many leading columns are part of the match. ref displays which column or constant is compared to that index, revealing why the index matched. A useful diagnostic step is to check possible_keys when key is NULL: if possible_keys is empty, you may need to create an index. If possible_keys lists an index but key is different or NULL, examine why the optimizer avoided it — sometimes column order in a composite index or data distribution matters. Avoid the mistake of assuming any index will be used; index design must match the WHERE and ORDER BY patterns. When you alter indexes, re-run EXPLAIN and confirm key changes from NULL to a named index and key_len shows expected usage of composite parts.

The rows column in EXPLAIN is an estimate of how many rows MySQL expects to examine to produce results for that table operation. Lower estimates generally indicate less work and lower cost. filtered expresses an estimated percentage of rows that pass the table-level condition; a higher filtered percentage is better because it means the condition is selective. These estimates come from table statistics and data distribution; they can be inaccurate if statistics are stale or data distribution is skewed. Use rows and filtered to prioritize fixes: an access type of range paired with millions in rows might still be a performance problem. A common mistake is to focus only on type and ignore rows; the combination of both gives a more accurate picture of cost. If rows is high, consider adding or refining indexes, rewriting the query, or adding more selective predicates. After making changes, refresh statistics and re-run EXPLAIN to confirm that rows and filtered improve, which usually translates into lower execution work when you subsequently run the query. rows and filtered: estimated work and selectivity means rows and filtered are optimizer estimates that guide where to apply indexing or query rewrites; always validate with real query runs after changes.. The Extra column often holds the clearest clues to hidden bottlenecks. "Using filesort" means MySQL must perform an extra pass to sort results because an index could not satisfy the ORDER BY. This can be expensive for large result sets. "Using temporary" indicates MySQL created a temporary table, frequently for GROUP BY or DISTINCT, and this can cause disk input and output if the temporary spills to disk. "Using index" is a positive flag meaning a covering index was used so the storage engine did not need to read full data rows. "Using where" simply means a WHERE clause was applied; when combined with ALL it tells you the engine applied the filter after scanning, which is inefficient. "Using index condition" shows that MySQL pushed down conditions into the storage engine to filter using the index, which can improve efficiency. A common trap is assuming Using index always means the plan is perfect; it indicates no row lookup was necessary but other tables or clauses may still be costly. Use the Extra column together with type and rows to diagnose and prioritize fixes like adding a composite index to eliminate filesort or avoid temporary table creation.
